what_its_for: Fluoxetine is used to treat depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), panic attacks, bulimia nervosa (an eating disorder), and premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). It belongs to a group of medicines called SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors), which work by helping balance a natural chemical in your brain called serotonin to improve your mood, sleep, appetite, and energy levels.
how_to_take: Take fluoxetine by mouth, with or without food. Swallow capsules whole — do not crush or chew them. Take it at the same time each day to help you remember. It is often taken in the morning because it can sometimes make it harder to fall asleep if taken at night. If you are taking the once-weekly capsule (Prozac Weekly), take it on the same day every week.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you. For most adults, the starting dose is usually 20 mg once a day. Your doctor may slowly increase your dose over time if needed, up to a maximum of 80 mg per day depending on your condition. Children and teenagers will be started on a lower dose. Always take the exact dose your doctor prescribed — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — UNLESS it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are taking the once-weekly capsule and miss a day, take it as soon as you remember, then go back to your regular weekly schedule.
storage: Store fluoxetine at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medication down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it safely.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking fluoxetine, as it can increase side effects like dizziness and drowsiness. Do NOT take fluoxetine if you have taken a MAO inhibitor (such as phenelzine, tranylcypromine, selegiline, or linezolid) in the last 14 days — this combination can cause a dangerous reaction. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medication affects you. Tell your doctor about ALL other medicines, supplements, and herbal products you take, especially blood thinners, other antidepressants, triptans for migraines, pain medicines, or St. John's Wort.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: thoughts of suicide or self-harm (especially in the first few weeks), new or worsening depression or anxiety, unusual changes in mood or behavior, seizures, high fever with stiff muscles or confusion (signs of serotonin syndrome), easy bruising or unusual bleeding, skin rash or hives, trouble breathing, or eye pain or vision changes. Also call your doctor if you feel you want to stop taking fluoxetine — stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms, and your doctor will help you taper off safely.
when_it_works: Fluoxetine does not work right away. You may start to notice some improvements in sleep, appetite, and energy within the first 1 to 2 weeks. However, it usually takes 4 to 6 weeks of regular use to feel the full benefit for mood and other symptoms. Some people may need up to 8 to 12 weeks. Do not stop taking it just because you do not feel better right away — be patient and keep taking it as directed. Talk to your doctor if you do not notice any improvement after several weeks.
special_populations: Children and Teenagers: Fluoxetine is approved for use in children aged 8 and older for depression, and age 7 and older for OCD. Parents and caregivers should watch children and teens closely for any changes in mood, behavior, or thoughts of self-harm, especially in the first few months of treatment. Elderly (65 and older): Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects, especially dizziness, low sodium levels, and falls. A lower starting dose may be used. Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Fluoxetine can pass into breast milk and may affect a nursing baby. Your doctor will help weigh the benefits and risks for you and your baby. Kidney or Liver Problems: If you have kidney or liver disease, your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more closely.
